# Setup

## Package Installation and Loading

We use `ordinal` for cumulative link mixed models (the central analytic workhorse),
`lme4` and `lmerTest` for the linear mixed model in H4, `emmeans` for pairwise 
comparisons, and standard tidyverse tools for data wrangling and visualization.

```{r packages}
# ── Install any missing packages ──
required_packages <- c(
  "tidyverse",    # data wrangling and plotting
  "ordinal",      # cumulative link mixed models (CLMM)
  "lme4",         # linear mixed models
  "lmerTest",     # p-values for lmer via Satterthwaite
  "emmeans",      # estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts
  "broom",        # tidy model summaries
  "broom.mixed",  # tidy summaries for mixed models
  "effectsize",   # standardized effect sizes
  "pwr",          # power calculations
  "knitr",        # tables
  "kableExtra",   # nicer tables
  "jsonlite",     # parse JSON strings (mpc_ranking column)
  "cluster",      # k-means clustering
  "factoextra",   # cluster visualization
  "geomtextpath", # text labels along curves (Jaime's suggestion)
  "pROC"          # ROC curves for threshold-specific models
)

for (pkg in required_packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org", quiet = TRUE)
  }
}

library(tidyverse)
library(ordinal)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)
library(effectsize)
library(pwr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(jsonlite)
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)
library(geomtextpath)
library(pROC)
# Note: MASS is installed but not loaded to avoid masking dplyr::select.
# We call MASS::mvrnorm() directly where needed.

# Seed for reproducibility in any bootstrapped or resampled procedures.
set.seed(2026)
```

## Formatting Helpers

A few small utility functions that get reused throughout.

```{r helpers}
# Convenience function: format p-values for inline reporting.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < .001) return("< .001")
  paste0("= ", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
}

# Convenience function: format a number to n decimal places, no leading zero.
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits)
}

# Design effect: adjusts effective sample size for within-subjects clustering.
#   DEFF = 1 + (k - 1) * ICC
#   where k = number of observations per cluster (here, 5 vignettes per person).
compute_deff <- function(icc, k = 5) {
  1 + (k - 1) * icc
}

# One-way ICC(1) from a simple ANOVA decomposition.
# This gives the proportion of total variance attributable to between-cluster
# (i.e., between-participant) differences.
compute_icc <- function(outcome, cluster_id) {
  fit <- aov(outcome ~ factor(cluster_id))
  ms <- summary(fit)[[1]]["Mean Sq"]
  ms_between <- ms[1, 1]
  ms_within  <- ms[2, 1]
  k <- mean(table(cluster_id))  # average cluster size
  icc <- (ms_between - ms_within) / (ms_between + (k - 1) * ms_within)
  max(icc, 0)  # floor at zero (negative ICC is not meaningful here)
}

# ── Color palette that degrades gracefully to grayscale ──
# Online readers see distinct colors; print readers distinguish by linetype.
# Colors chosen to be colorblind-safe (Wong palette) and remain separable
# when desaturated to grayscale.
judgment_colors <- c(
  "Blamelessness" = "#0072B2",   # blue
  "Negligence"    = "#D55E00",   # vermilion/orange
  "Recklessness"  = "#009E73",   # teal/green
  "Knowledge"     = "#CC79A7"    # pink/mauve
)
judgment_grays <- c(
  "Blamelessness" = "grey75",
  "Negligence"    = "grey50",
  "Recklessness"  = "grey25",
  "Knowledge"     = "black"
)
judgment_linetypes <- c(
  "Blamelessness" = "dotted",
  "Negligence"    = "dashed",
  "Recklessness"  = "solid",
  "Knowledge"     = "twodash"
)

# Helper: save both color and grayscale versions of a publication figure.
save_dual <- function(fig_color, fig_bw, basename, width, height) {
  ggsave(paste0(basename, ".pdf"), fig_color, width = width, height = height)
  ggsave(paste0(basename, "_bw.pdf"), fig_bw, width = width, height = height)
  cat("Saved:", paste0(basename, ".pdf"), "and", paste0(basename, "_bw.pdf"), "\n")
}
```


# Data Loading and Cleaning

```{r load-data}
# ── Read the combined CSV ──
# Each row is one trial: one participant × one vignette.
# Participants each completed 5 vignettes, so the data is clustered.
DATA_PATH <- "/Users/dgkamper/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-dgkamper@gmail.com/My Drive/DGK Lab/Reasoning Lab/DGK Lab - Mens Rea /Data/modeling_mental_states_analysis_part3.csv"
raw <- read_csv(DATA_PATH, show_col_types = FALSE)

# ── Normalize factor levels ──
# The CoWork processing script introduced "$1,000 " (with comma and trailing
# space) in place of the original "$1000". Standardise to the label the
# ifelse() calls downstream expect.
raw <- raw %>%
  mutate(payment = case_when(
    str_detect(payment, "1.?000") ~ "$1000",
    TRUE ~ trimws(payment)
  ))

cat("Raw dataset:", nrow(raw), "rows,", n_distinct(raw$session_id), "unique session IDs\n")
cat("Payment levels after normalisation:", paste(sort(unique(raw$payment)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r exclusions}
# ── Exclusion criteria ──
# 1. Drop participants who did not complete all 5 vignettes.
# 2. Drop duplicate session IDs if any exist.
# These decisions are made blind to judgment content (per preregistration).

completions <- raw %>%
  group_by(session_id) %>%
  summarise(n_trials = n(), .groups = "drop")

# How many participants completed fewer than 5?
incomplete <- completions %>% filter(n_trials < 5)
cat("Participants with < 5 trials:", nrow(incomplete), "\n")
if (nrow(incomplete) > 0) print(incomplete)

# Keep only complete cases
complete_ids <- completions %>% filter(n_trials == 5) %>% pull(session_id)
d <- raw %>% filter(session_id %in% complete_ids)

cat("\nPost-exclusion:", nrow(d), "trials from", n_distinct(d$session_id), "participants\n")
```

```{r derive-variables}
# ── Derive analysis variables ──

# Ordinal culpability score: maps the four MPC categories onto a numeric scale
# that respects the legal hierarchy. This is the primary DV for the CLMMs.
culp_map <- c("Blamelessness" = 1, "Negligence" = 2, 
              "Recklessness" = 3, "Knowledge" = 4)
d <- d %>%
  mutate(
    # Numeric culpability (1-4) and ordered factor version
    culpability   = culp_map[judgment],
    culpability_f = factor(culpability, levels = 1:4, ordered = TRUE),
    
    # Participant ID as a factor for random effects
    pid = factor(session_id),
    
    # Binary vignette features: code each as 0/1 for regression.
    # The "1" level is the theoretically more incriminating or salient option.
    # This coding means positive coefficients indicate that the "1" level
    # pushes judgments toward higher culpability.
    source_bin   = ifelse(source == "biker", 1, 0),
    package_bin  = ifelse(package == "duffel_bag", 1, 0),
    inquiry_bin  = ifelse(inquiry == "source_tells", 1, 0),
    payment_bin  = ifelse(payment == "$1000", 1, 0),
    location_bin = ifelse(location == "Mexico", 1, 0),
    contents_bin = ifelse(contents == "fentanyl", 1, 0),
    
    # Center the risk slider around its grand mean for easier interpretation
    # of intercepts in the mixed models.
    risk_c = slider_value - mean(slider_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Vignette presentation position (1-5), useful for order effects.
    position = as.integer(vignette_position)
  )

# ── Parse MPC ranking data ──
# The mpc_ranking column is a JSON array like ["Knowledge","Recklessness",...].
# Each participant ranked the four definitions from most to least culpable.
# We only need one row per participant for this, so we extract it separately.

ranking_data <- d %>%
  distinct(pid, mpc_ranking) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mpc_ranking)) %>%
  mutate(
    ranking = map(mpc_ranking, ~ fromJSON(.x)),
    # The correct MPC ordering (most to least culpable):
    correct_order = list(c("Knowledge", "Recklessness", "Negligence", "Blamelessness")),
    # Did they get the exact ordering right?
    exact_match   = map2_lgl(ranking, correct_order, ~ identical(.x, .y)),
    # Did they get the endpoints right? (Knowledge first, Blamelessness last)
    endpoints_correct = map_lgl(ranking, ~ .x[1] == "Knowledge" & .x[4] == "Blamelessness")
  )

# ── Parse RPM data ──
# Each participant answered 5 RPM items. rpm_correct is the total correct.
rpm_data <- d %>%
  distinct(pid, rpm_correct, rpm_total) %>%
  filter(!is.na(rpm_correct)) %>%
  mutate(rpm_prop = rpm_correct / rpm_total)

# Merge RPM proportion back into the main dataset for use as a covariate.
d <- d %>%
  left_join(rpm_data %>% dplyr::select(pid, rpm_prop), by = "pid")

cat("Analysis dataset ready.\n")
cat("  Participants:", n_distinct(d$pid), "\n")
cat("  Trials:", nrow(d), "\n")
cat("  Judgments:", paste(names(table(d$judgment)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## Intraclass Correlations

The ICC tells us how much of the variance in each outcome is due to stable
between-person differences versus genuine trial-to-trial variation. This is
essential for computing the design effect, which in turn determines how much
the within-subjects clustering inflates our effective sample size.

```{r icc}
icc_slider <- compute_icc(d$slider_value, d$pid)
icc_culp   <- compute_icc(d$culpability, d$pid)

deff_slider <- compute_deff(icc_slider)
deff_culp   <- compute_deff(icc_culp)

tibble(
  Measure = c("Risk Slider (0–100)", "Culpability Score (1–4)"),
  ICC     = c(icc_slider, icc_culp),
  `Design Effect` = c(deff_slider, deff_culp),
  `Effective N (trials)` = round(nrow(d) / c(deff_slider, deff_culp))
) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Intraclass correlations and design effects") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

# Hypothesis Tests

## H1: Non-Uniform Distribution of Judgments

If participants are merely guessing or treating the four categories as
interchangeable, we would expect a uniform distribution (25% per category).
H1 predicts systematic deviation from uniformity.

```{r h1-chi-square}
# ── Trial-level chi-square ──
# This is the straightforward test on all trials, but it treats each trial
# as an independent observation. With 5 trials per person and non-trivial
# ICC, the effective sample size is smaller than the raw trial count.

observed <- table(d$judgment)
n_trials <- sum(observed)
expected <- rep(n_trials / 4, 4)

chi_test <- chisq.test(observed, p = rep(0.25, 4))

# Cohen's w: effect size for the chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
# w = sqrt(chi2 / N), but we need to use the DEFF-adjusted N for
# a fair comparison.
cohens_w <- sqrt(chi_test$statistic / n_trials)

# DEFF-adjusted chi-square: the test statistic scales linearly with N,
# so dividing by the design effect gives the corrected statistic.
chi_adj <- chi_test$statistic / deff_culp
p_adj   <- pchisq(chi_adj, df = 3, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat("── H1: Chi-square goodness-of-fit ──\n")
cat("Observed: ", paste(names(observed), "=", observed, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Expected (uniform): ", round(expected[1]), "each\n\n")
cat("Uncorrected:  χ²(3) =", round(chi_test$statistic, 2), 
    ", p", fmt_p(chi_test$p.value), "\n")
cat("DEFF-adjusted: χ²(3) =", round(chi_adj, 2),
    ", p", fmt_p(p_adj), "\n")
cat("Cohen's w =", fmt_num(cohens_w, 3), "\n")
```

```{r h1-follow-up}
# ── Follow-up: pairwise comparisons ──
# Which categories are over- or under-represented relative to 25%?
# We use one-sample proportion tests with Holm correction.

categories <- c("Blamelessness", "Negligence", "Recklessness", "Knowledge")
pairwise_h1 <- map_dfr(categories, function(cat) {
  k   <- sum(d$judgment == cat)
  n   <- nrow(d)
  tst <- prop.test(k, n, p = 0.25)
  tibble(
    Category     = cat,
    Observed_Pct = k / n * 100,
    Expected_Pct = 25,
    Chi2         = tst$statistic,
    p_uncorrected = tst$p.value
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_uncorrected, method = "holm"))

pairwise_h1 %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 1, 0, 2, 4, 4),
        caption = "H1 follow-up: each category vs. 25% uniform baseline") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

**Interpretation.** Even after correcting for within-subjects clustering via the
design effect, the chi-square test is highly significant, confirming that 
participants do not distribute their judgments uniformly. Negligence is
overselected and Knowledge is underselected relative to the uniform baseline.
Recklessness is the only category not significantly different from 25%.


## H2: Risk Magnitude Predicts Culpability

This is the core prediction of the MPC framework: if participants are sensitive
to the legally relevant distinction between mental states, then higher perceived 
risk should map onto higher culpability judgments.

### Spearman Correlation

```{r h2-spearman}
# ── Spearman rank correlation ──
# This is a nonparametric test of the monotonic association between the
# continuous risk slider (0–100) and the ordinal culpability score (1–4).
# Note: this is computed at the trial level and does not account for
# clustering. We report the DEFF-adjusted effective N for context.

rho_test <- cor.test(d$slider_value, d$culpability, method = "spearman",
                     exact = FALSE)

cat("── H2: Spearman correlation ──\n")
cat("ρ =", fmt_num(rho_test$estimate, 3), "\n")
cat("S =", round(rho_test$statistic), ", p", fmt_p(rho_test$p.value), "\n")
cat("(Trial-level; effective N after DEFF correction ≈", 
    round(nrow(d) / deff_slider), ")\n")
```

### Cumulative Link Mixed Model: Risk Only

The CLMM is the primary parametric test for H2. It models the ordinal
culpability score (1 = Blamelessness through 4 = Knowledge) as a function
of the continuous risk slider, with a random intercept for each participant
to account for the repeated-measures structure. The CLMM extends standard
ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds model) by incorporating
random effects that account for the non-independence of observations within
participants. A standard ordinal regression would treat all 1,060 trials as
independent, ignoring the clustering of 5 trials per person and inflating
Type I error rates. The CLMM handles this by estimating participant-specific
intercepts, yielding correctly calibrated standard errors and valid inference
despite the within-subjects design.

The cumulative link model assumes proportional odds: the effect of risk on
the log-odds of being in a higher culpability category is constant across
the three threshold transitions (1→2, 2→3, 3→4). This is tested later
in the diagnostics section.

```{r h2-clmm}
# ── Fit the risk-only CLMM ──
m_risk <- clmm(culpability_f ~ slider_value + (1 | pid), data = d)

cat("── H2: Cumulative Link Mixed Model (risk only) ──\n")
summary(m_risk)
```

```{r h2-clmm-interpretation}
# Extract and interpret the risk coefficient.
coef_risk <- summary(m_risk)$coefficients
risk_row  <- coef_risk["slider_value", ]

# The raw coefficient is in log-odds per unit change in slider_value.
# Since slider_value ranges 0–100, a one-unit change is small. We also
# compute the standardized coefficient (log-odds per 1 SD of slider).
risk_b   <- risk_row["Estimate"]
risk_se  <- risk_row["Std. Error"]
risk_z   <- risk_row["z value"]
risk_p   <- risk_row["Pr(>|z|)"]
risk_b_std <- risk_b * sd(d$slider_value)

cat("Risk coefficient: b =", fmt_num(risk_b, 4), 
    ", SE =", fmt_num(risk_se, 4),
    ", z =", fmt_num(risk_z, 2),
    ", p", fmt_p(risk_p), "\n")
cat("Standardized: β =", fmt_num(risk_b_std, 3),
    "(log-odds per 1 SD of slider)\n")
cat("Odds ratio per 10-point slider increase:", 
    fmt_num(exp(risk_b * 10), 3), "\n")
```

### Predicted Probability Curves

These curves show how the predicted probability of each mental state category
changes as a function of the risk slider, holding random effects at zero
(i.e., for an "average" participant). We include 95% parametric bootstrap
confidence bands computed from the variance-covariance matrix of the CLMM
estimates.

```{r predicted-probabilities, fig.height=5}
# ── Compute predicted probabilities from the CLMM ──
# The cumulative link model gives us thresholds (α_j) and a slope (β).
# P(Y ≤ j | x) = logistic(α_j - β * x)
# P(Y = j | x) = P(Y ≤ j) - P(Y ≤ j-1)

thresholds <- m_risk$Theta           # three threshold parameters
beta       <- coef(m_risk)["slider_value"]

slider_seq <- seq(0, 100, by = 1)

# ── Point estimates ──
pred_probs <- map_dfr(slider_seq, function(x) {
  cum_probs <- plogis(thresholds - beta * x)
  probs <- c(cum_probs[1],
             cum_probs[2] - cum_probs[1],
             cum_probs[3] - cum_probs[2],
             1 - cum_probs[3])
  tibble(
    slider = x,
    Blamelessness = probs[1],
    Negligence    = probs[2],
    Recklessness  = probs[3],
    Knowledge     = probs[4]
  )
}) %>%
  pivot_longer(-slider, names_to = "judgment", values_to = "probability") %>%
  mutate(judgment = factor(judgment,
    levels = c("Blamelessness","Negligence","Recklessness","Knowledge")))

# ── Parametric bootstrap confidence bands ──
# We draw from the multivariate normal distribution of the estimated
# parameters (thresholds + slope) using the model's variance-covariance
# matrix, then compute predicted probabilities under each draw. The 2.5th
# and 97.5th percentiles across draws give 95% confidence bands.

n_boot <- 1000

# The vcov() method for clmm returns only the fixed-effect vcov (1×1 here).
# The Hessian includes ALL parameters: thresholds, fixed effects, AND the
# random effect variance. We need the joint vcov of just the thresholds
# and fixed effects (first 4 parameters), marginalizing over the random
# effect variance.
param_est <- c(m_risk$Theta, coef(m_risk)["slider_value"])
n_params  <- length(param_est)  # should be 4

# Invert the full Hessian, then extract the submatrix for our 4 parameters.
full_vcov <- solve(m_risk$Hessian)
# The Hessian row/col order is: thresholds, fixed effects, random effects.
# We take only the first n_params rows and columns.
vcov_sub <- full_vcov[1:n_params, 1:n_params]

# Draw parameter samples from the joint multivariate normal.
boot_params <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_boot, mu = param_est, Sigma = vcov_sub)

# For each draw, compute predicted probabilities at each slider value.
boot_probs <- array(NA, dim = c(n_boot, length(slider_seq), 4))
for (b in 1:n_boot) {
  th_b   <- boot_params[b, 1:3]
  beta_b <- boot_params[b, 4]
  for (i in seq_along(slider_seq)) {
    x <- slider_seq[i]
    cum_b <- plogis(th_b - beta_b * x)
    boot_probs[b, i, ] <- c(cum_b[1],
                              cum_b[2] - cum_b[1],
                              cum_b[3] - cum_b[2],
                              1 - cum_b[3])
  }
}

# Extract 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles for each category × slider value.
ci_data <- map_dfr(1:4, function(j) {
  lo <- apply(boot_probs[, , j], 2, quantile, probs = 0.025)
  hi <- apply(boot_probs[, , j], 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)
  tibble(
    slider  = slider_seq,
    ci_lo   = lo,
    ci_hi   = hi,
    judgment = c("Blamelessness","Negligence","Recklessness","Knowledge")[j]
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(judgment = factor(judgment,
    levels = c("Blamelessness","Negligence","Recklessness","Knowledge")))

# Merge point estimates with CIs.
pred_with_ci <- pred_probs %>%
  left_join(ci_data, by = c("slider", "judgment"))

ggplot(pred_with_ci, aes(x = slider, y = probability, 
                         color = judgment, linetype = judgment)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi, fill = judgment, group = judgment),
              alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = judgment_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = judgment_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = judgment_linetypes) +
  labs(x = "Risk Slider (0–100)",
       y = "Predicted Probability",
       color = "Mental State", linetype = "Mental State") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


## H3: Extralegal Feature Bias

H3 tests whether vignette surface features influence culpability judgments
even after controlling for perceived risk. The CLMM from H2 is extended
to include all six binary vignette features as fixed effects.

### Full CLMM: Risk + Features

```{r h3-clmm-features}
# ── Fit the full model: risk + all six features ──
# The features are coded 0/1 with the more incriminating level as 1:
#   source_bin:   biker = 1 (vs. uncle)
#   package_bin:  duffel_bag = 1 (vs. gift-wrapped)
#   inquiry_bin:  source_tells = 1 (vs. defendant asks)
#   payment_bin:  $1000 = 1 (vs. none)
#   location_bin: Mexico = 1 (vs. Canada)
#   contents_bin: fentanyl = 1 (vs. rare disease drugs)

m_full <- clmm(
  culpability_f ~ slider_value + source_bin + package_bin + inquiry_bin +
                  payment_bin + location_bin + contents_bin + (1 | pid),
  data = d
)

cat("── H3: Full CLMM (risk + features) ──\n")
summary(m_full)
```

```{r h3-feature-table}
# ── Extract feature coefficients ──
coefs <- summary(m_full)$coefficients

# We only want the predictor coefficients, not the thresholds.
predictor_names <- c("slider_value", "source_bin", "package_bin", 
                     "inquiry_bin", "payment_bin", "location_bin", "contents_bin")

# Sanity check: verify all expected predictors appear in the model output.
missing <- setdiff(predictor_names, rownames(coefs))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  cat("WARNING: the following predictors are missing from the model output:\n")
  cat(" ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("Available coefficient names:", paste(rownames(coefs), collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("This usually means a predictor became constant (all 0 or all 1).\n")
  cat("Check factor levels in the data before proceeding.\n\n")
  # Fall back to whatever predictors DO exist so the document can still knit.
  predictor_names <- intersect(predictor_names, rownames(coefs))
}

feature_table <- as_tibble(coefs[predictor_names, ], rownames = "Predictor") %>%
  rename(b = Estimate, SE = `Std. Error`, z = `z value`, p = `Pr(>|z|)`) %>%
  mutate(
    OR = exp(b),
    # Convert log-odds coefficient to approximate Cohen's d using the
    # logistic distribution variance (pi^2/3). For binary predictors,
    # d ≈ b * sqrt(3) / pi.
    d_approx = ifelse(Predictor != "slider_value", b * sqrt(3) / pi, NA)
  )

# ── Holm correction: applied only to the 6 features, not to risk ──
# Risk is tested under H2; the features are a separate family for H3.
feature_only <- feature_table %>% filter(Predictor != "slider_value")
feature_only$p_holm <- p.adjust(feature_only$p, method = "holm")
feature_only <- feature_only %>%
  mutate(Sig = case_when(
    p_holm < .001  ~ "***",
    p_holm < .01   ~ "**",
    p_holm < .05   ~ "*",
    p      < .05   ~ "†",    # uncorrected significant, Holm-corrected not
    TRUE           ~ ""
  ))

risk_only_row <- feature_table %>% 
  filter(Predictor == "slider_value") %>%
  mutate(
    p_holm = NA_real_,
    Sig = case_when(p < .001 ~ "***", p < .01 ~ "**", p < .05 ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")
  )

feature_table <- bind_rows(risk_only_row, feature_only)

# Readable labels
feature_table <- feature_table %>%
  mutate(Predictor = recode(Predictor,
    "slider_value" = "Risk Slider",
    "source_bin"   = "Source (biker)",
    "package_bin"  = "Package (duffel bag)",
    "inquiry_bin"  = "Inquiry (source tells)",
    "payment_bin"  = "Payment ($1000)",
    "location_bin" = "Location (Mexico)",
    "contents_bin" = "Contents (fentanyl)"
  ))

feature_table %>%
  dplyr::select(Predictor, b, SE, z, p, OR, d_approx, p_holm, Sig) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 3, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 4, 0),
        col.names = c("Predictor", "b", "SE", "z", "p", "OR", "d (approx)", 
                       "p (Holm)", ""),
        caption = "H3: Full CLMM coefficients († = uncorrected p < .05 only)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

**Feature interpretation.** Payment ($1000 vs. none) is the only feature
that survives Holm correction, with an odds ratio of 1.70 and an approximate
Cohen's d in the small-to-medium range. Source (biker vs. uncle) shows a
marginal trend at the uncorrected level that does not survive multiple
comparison correction even with the full sample of 212 participants and
1,060 trials. The remaining four features (package type, inquiry direction,
location, and contents) show no meaningful effects, confirming that
participants' mental state attributions are driven primarily by perceived risk
and financial motive rather than by geographic stereotypes, outcome severity,
or other surface features of the scenario.

### Forest Plot of Feature Effects

```{r forest-plot, fig.height=5}
# ── Forest plot: feature coefficients with 95% CIs ──
forest_data <- feature_table %>%
  filter(Predictor != "Risk Slider") %>%
  mutate(
    ci_lo = b - 1.96 * SE,
    ci_hi = b + 1.96 * SE,
    Predictor = factor(Predictor, levels = rev(Predictor))
  )

ggplot(forest_data, aes(x = b, y = Predictor)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi), height = 0.2, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Log-Odds Coefficient (95% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

### Model Comparison

```{r model-comparison}
# ── Compare nested models ──
# Model 1: risk only (H2)
# Model 2: risk + features (H3)
# The likelihood ratio test tells us whether the features as a group
# add significantly to the model beyond risk alone.

lr_test <- anova(m_risk, m_full)
cat("── Model comparison: risk-only vs. risk + features ──\n")
print(lr_test)
```

### Random Slopes Model

We also fit a model that allows the risk slope to vary across participants.
This is more theoretically complete (different people may weight risk
differently), but with only 5 observations per person it may struggle
to converge.

```{r random-slopes}
# ── Try random slopes for risk ──
# If this doesn't converge, we fall back to random-intercepts-only.
m_full_slopes <- tryCatch({
  clmm(
    culpability_f ~ slider_value + source_bin + package_bin + inquiry_bin +
                    payment_bin + location_bin + contents_bin +
                    (1 + slider_value | pid),
    data = d
  )
}, warning = function(w) {
  cat("Warning during random-slopes fit:", conditionMessage(w), "\n")
  suppressWarnings(
    clmm(
      culpability_f ~ slider_value + source_bin + package_bin + inquiry_bin +
                      payment_bin + location_bin + contents_bin +
                      (1 + slider_value | pid),
      data = d
    )
  )
}, error = function(e) {
  cat("Random slopes model failed to converge:", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
  cat("Falling back to random-intercepts-only model.\n")
  NULL
})

if (!is.null(m_full_slopes)) {
  # ── Check convergence ──
  # The ordinal package stores convergence info in varying field names
  # depending on version. We check several possibilities.
  cat("── Random slopes model ──\n")
  
  max_grad <- m_full_slopes$maxGradient
  if (!is.numeric(max_grad)) max_grad <- m_full_slopes$info$max.grad
  if (!is.numeric(max_grad)) {
    # Print whatever convergence info we can find
    cat("Convergence info from model:\n")
    str(m_full_slopes$convergence)
    cat("\n")
  } else {
    cat("Max |gradient|:", fmt_num(max_grad, 6), "\n")
    cat("Gradient acceptable (< 1e-03):", max_grad < 1e-03, "\n")
  }
  cat("\n")
  
  # ── Compare with random-intercepts-only ──
  lr_slopes <- anova(m_full, m_full_slopes)
  print(lr_slopes)
  
  # ── Random effects variance components ──
  cat("\nRandom effects:\n")
  vc <- VarCorr(m_full_slopes)
  print(vc)
  
  # ── Interpret the intercept-slope correlation ──
  # A strong negative correlation means that participants who start with
  # higher baseline culpability (harsher judges) show flatter risk slopes:
  # they are less sensitive to variation in perceived risk. Conversely,
  # participants with low baselines (more lenient) show steeper slopes,
  # meaning they differentiate more sharply by risk.
  rs_corr <- tryCatch({
    attr(vc$pid, "correlation")[1, 2]
  }, error = function(e) {
    # If the structure is different, try the correlation matrix directly
    tryCatch(vc$pid[1, 2] / sqrt(vc$pid[1, 1] * vc$pid[2, 2]),
             error = function(e2) NA_real_)
  })
  
  if (!is.na(rs_corr)) {
    cat("\nIntercept–slope correlation:", fmt_num(rs_corr, 3), "\n")
    if (abs(rs_corr) > 0.85) {
      cat("NOTE: This correlation is very high (|r| > .85), which raises\n")
      cat("concerns about overparameterization. With only 5 observations per\n")
      cat("participant, the random slopes structure may not be estimable with\n")
      cat("precision. The significant LRT improvement indicates meaningfully\n")
      cat("better fit, but the specific variance component estimates should\n")
      cat("be interpreted cautiously. The substantive implication — that\n")
      cat("harsher judges are less risk-sensitive — is a plausible individual\n")
      cat("difference pattern, but the extreme correlation value (|r| > .85)\n")
      cat("suggests the model is likely overparameterized given the limited\n")
      cat("within-person observations. The random-intercepts-only model should\n")
      cat("be preferred for inference on the fixed effects.\n")
    }
  }
} else {
  cat("Random slopes model did not converge. Using random-intercepts-only.\n")
}
```


## H4: Risk Distinguishes Recklessness from Knowledge (Exploratory)

Among trials classified as Recklessness or Knowledge, does the risk slider
distinguish between them? Under the MPC, Knowledge requires near-certainty
of the outcome, while Recklessness requires only awareness of a substantial
risk. If participants draw this distinction, Knowledge trials should have
higher risk ratings.

```{r h4-rk-lmm}
# ── Subset to R and K trials ──
d_rk <- d %>%
  filter(judgment %in% c("Recklessness", "Knowledge")) %>%
  mutate(is_knowledge = ifelse(judgment == "Knowledge", 1, 0))

cat("── H4: R vs. K ──\n")
cat("Recklessness trials:", sum(d_rk$is_knowledge == 0), "\n")
cat("Knowledge trials:", sum(d_rk$is_knowledge == 1), "\n\n")

# ── Descriptive comparison ──
rk_desc <- d_rk %>%
  group_by(judgment) %>%
  summarise(
    n    = n(),
    mean = mean(slider_value),
    sd   = sd(slider_value),
    se   = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
print(rk_desc)

# ── Linear mixed model ──
# risk ~ is_knowledge + (1 | pid)
# This accounts for the fact that the same participant can contribute
# both R and K trials (for different vignettes).
m_rk <- lmer(slider_value ~ is_knowledge + (1 | pid), data = d_rk)

cat("\n── LMM: slider_value ~ is_knowledge + (1 | pid) ──\n")
summary(m_rk)

# Effect size: Cohen's d from the LMM coefficient
rk_coef <- summary(m_rk)$coefficients["is_knowledge", ]
pooled_sd <- sd(d_rk$slider_value)
cohens_d_rk <- rk_coef["Estimate"] / pooled_sd

cat("\nCohen's d =", fmt_num(cohens_d_rk, 3), "\n")
cat("Direction:", ifelse(rk_coef["Estimate"] > 0, 
    "Knowledge > Recklessness (expected)", 
    "Knowledge < Recklessness (REVERSED)"), "\n")

# ── Two-tailed and one-tailed tests ──
# We preregistered a one-tailed test (Knowledge > Recklessness), but given
# the reversed direction, both tests are reported for transparency.
t_val <- rk_coef["t value"]
df_val <- summary(m_rk)$coefficients["is_knowledge", "df"]
p_two_tailed <- 2 * pt(abs(t_val), df = df_val, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_one_tailed <- pt(t_val, df = df_val, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat("Two-tailed p", fmt_p(p_two_tailed), "\n")
cat("One-tailed p (preregistered: K > R)", fmt_p(p_one_tailed), "\n")
```

**Interpretation.** The effect is significantly reversed: participants assigned
*lower* risk ratings to trials they classified as Knowledge than to those
classified as Recklessness. This reversal is consistent with the proportional
odds violation documented in the diagnostics section below, where the risk
coefficient at the Knowledge threshold is substantially attenuated relative to
lower thresholds. Together, these findings indicate that participants' use of
the Knowledge category is not primarily driven by high perceived risk. Rather,
Knowledge judgments appear to be triggered by qualitative features of the
vignettes (most notably payment) or by a categorical inference about the
defendant's state of mind that is not captured by the continuous risk slider.
With 286 Recklessness and 145 Knowledge trials, this reversal is robust and
unlikely to be an artifact of insufficient power.


# Secondary and Exploratory Analyses

## MPC Ranking Accuracy

After the five vignette trials, participants ranked the four mental state
definitions from most to least culpable. We test whether they can recover
the correct MPC ordering when the definitions are presented side by side.

```{r mpc-ranking}
cat("── MPC Ranking Accuracy ──\n")
cat("Participants with ranking data:", nrow(ranking_data), "\n")
cat("Exact correct (K > R > N > B):", sum(ranking_data$exact_match),
    "(", round(mean(ranking_data$exact_match) * 100, 1), "%)\n")
cat("Endpoints correct (K first, B last):", sum(ranking_data$endpoints_correct),
    "(", round(mean(ranking_data$endpoints_correct) * 100, 1), "%)\n")

# ── Binomial test against chance ──
# With 4 items, there are 4! = 24 possible orderings. Chance = 1/24 ≈ 4.17%.
n_correct <- sum(ranking_data$exact_match)
n_total   <- nrow(ranking_data)
binom_test <- binom.test(n_correct, n_total, p = 1/24, alternative = "greater")

cat("\nBinomial test (exact match vs. chance = 4.17%):\n")
cat("  Observed:", n_correct, "/", n_total, 
    "(", round(n_correct / n_total * 100, 1), "%)\n")
cat("  p", fmt_p(binom_test$p.value), "\n")
cat("  95% CI:", round(binom_test$conf.int[1] * 100, 1), "% –",
    round(binom_test$conf.int[2] * 100, 1), "%\n")

# ── Endpoints binomial test ──
# Chance of getting both endpoints right by chance:
# P(K first) = 1/4, P(B last | K first) = 1/3, so P(both) = 1/12 ≈ 8.33%.
n_endpoints <- sum(ranking_data$endpoints_correct)
binom_endpoints <- binom.test(n_endpoints, n_total, p = 1/12, alternative = "greater")

cat("\nEndpoints test (K first & B last vs. chance = 8.33%):\n")
cat("  Observed:", n_endpoints, "/", n_total,
    "(", round(n_endpoints / n_total * 100, 1), "%)\n")
cat("  p", fmt_p(binom_endpoints$p.value), "\n")
```

```{r kendall-tau}
# ── Kendall's tau for each participant ──
# This gives a continuous measure of how close each participant's ranking
# is to the correct ordering, rather than the all-or-nothing exact match.

correct_numeric <- c("Knowledge" = 1, "Recklessness" = 2, 
                     "Negligence" = 3, "Blamelessness" = 4)

ranking_data <- ranking_data %>%
  mutate(
    participant_numeric = map(ranking, ~ correct_numeric[.x]),
    tau = map_dbl(participant_numeric, ~ cor(.x, 1:4, method = "kendall"))
  )

cat("── Kendall's τ ──\n")
cat("Mean τ:", fmt_num(mean(ranking_data$tau), 3), "\n")
cat("SD τ:", fmt_num(sd(ranking_data$tau), 3), "\n")

# Test whether the mean tau is significantly above zero (random ranking).
tau_test <- t.test(ranking_data$tau, mu = 0, alternative = "greater")
cat("One-sample t-test (H0: τ = 0):\n")
cat("  t(", tau_test$parameter, ") =", fmt_num(tau_test$statistic, 2),
    ", p", fmt_p(tau_test$p.value), "\n")
```


## RPM and Cognitive Ability Moderation

Does cognitive ability (proxied by Raven's Progressive Matrices performance)
moderate the relationship between risk perception and culpability judgment?

```{r rpm-descriptives}
cat("── RPM Descriptives ──\n")
cat("Mean correct:", fmt_num(mean(rpm_data$rpm_correct, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    "out of", rpm_data$rpm_total[1], "\n")
cat("SD:", fmt_num(sd(rpm_data$rpm_correct, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("Range:", min(rpm_data$rpm_correct, na.rm = TRUE), "–", 
    max(rpm_data$rpm_correct, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
```

```{r rpm-moderation}
# ── CLMM with RPM interaction ──
# risk * rpm_prop tests whether the risk–culpability slope is steeper
# for participants with higher cognitive ability.

# Center RPM for interpretability
d <- d %>%
  mutate(rpm_c = rpm_prop - mean(rpm_prop, na.rm = TRUE))

m_rpm <- clmm(
  culpability_f ~ slider_value * rpm_c + source_bin + package_bin +
                  inquiry_bin + payment_bin + location_bin + contents_bin +
                  (1 | pid),
  data = d %>% filter(!is.na(rpm_c))
)

cat("── RPM × Risk Interaction ──\n")
summary(m_rpm)

# Test the interaction term specifically.
rpm_coefs <- summary(m_rpm)$coefficients
if ("slider_value:rpm_c" %in% rownames(rpm_coefs)) {
  interaction_row <- rpm_coefs["slider_value:rpm_c", ]
  cat("\nInteraction (slider × RPM):\n")
  cat("  b =", fmt_num(interaction_row["Estimate"], 4),
      ", z =", fmt_num(interaction_row["z value"], 2),
      ", p", fmt_p(interaction_row["Pr(>|z|)"]), "\n")
  if (abs(interaction_row["Pr(>|z|)"]) > .05) {
    cat("  Interpretation: The interaction is not significant, indicating\n")
    cat("  that cognitive ability (RPM) does not moderate the relationship\n")
    cat("  between risk perception and culpability judgment.\n")
  } else if (interaction_row["Estimate"] > 0) {
    cat("  Interpretation: The positive interaction means higher-RPM participants\n")
    cat("  show a steeper risk–culpability slope — they differentiate more\n")
    cat("  sharply between mental states on the basis of perceived risk.\n")
  } else {
    cat("  Interpretation: The negative interaction means higher-RPM participants\n")
    cat("  show a shallower risk–culpability slope — they differentiate less\n")
    cat("  sharply between mental states on the basis of perceived risk.\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("\nWARNING: slider_value:rpm_c interaction not found in model output.\n")
  cat("Available terms:", paste(rownames(rpm_coefs), collapse = ", "), "\n")
}
```

```{r rpm-ranking-correlation}
# ── Does RPM predict ranking accuracy? ──
ranking_rpm <- ranking_data %>%
  left_join(rpm_data, by = "pid") %>%
  filter(!is.na(rpm_prop))

# Point-biserial correlation: RPM proportion correct × exact match
if (sum(ranking_rpm$exact_match) > 2) {
  rpm_rank_cor <- cor.test(ranking_rpm$rpm_prop, 
                           as.numeric(ranking_rpm$exact_match))
  cat("RPM × exact ranking match: r =", fmt_num(rpm_rank_cor$estimate, 3),
      ", p", fmt_p(rpm_rank_cor$p.value), "\n")
}

# Correlation with Kendall's tau (continuous ranking quality)
rpm_tau_cor <- cor.test(ranking_rpm$rpm_prop, ranking_rpm$tau)
cat("RPM × Kendall's τ: r =", fmt_num(rpm_tau_cor$estimate, 3),
    ", p", fmt_p(rpm_tau_cor$p.value), "\n")
```


## Individual Differences Clustering

We look for participant-level profiles that might reveal distinct "types"
of judgment strategy (e.g., consistently harsh, consistently lenient,
risk-calibrated, or random-looking).

```{r clustering-profiles}
# ── Build participant-level feature vectors ──
participant_profiles <- d %>%
  group_by(pid) %>%
  summarise(
    # Judgment distribution: proportion of trials in each category
    pct_B = mean(judgment == "Blamelessness"),
    pct_N = mean(judgment == "Negligence"),
    pct_R = mean(judgment == "Recklessness"),
    pct_K = mean(judgment == "Knowledge"),
    # Mean and SD of risk slider
    mean_risk = mean(slider_value),
    sd_risk   = sd(slider_value),
    # Within-person risk-culpability correlation
    rho_risk_culp = cor(slider_value, culpability, method = "spearman"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(ranking_data %>% dplyr::select(pid, tau, exact_match), by = "pid") %>%
  left_join(rpm_data %>% dplyr::select(pid, rpm_prop), by = "pid") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))

# ── K-means clustering ──
# We use the judgment proportions + mean risk + rho as the clustering features.
# RPM and tau are held out as validation variables.
cluster_vars <- participant_profiles %>%
  dplyr::select(pct_B, pct_N, pct_R, pct_K, mean_risk, rho_risk_culp) %>%
  scale()

# Determine optimal k using the silhouette method.
sil_results <- map_dbl(2:6, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(cluster_vars, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
  mean(silhouette(km$cluster, dist(cluster_vars))[, "sil_width"])
})

optimal_k <- which.max(sil_results) + 1  # +1 because we started at k=2
cat("Silhouette widths for k = 2 through 6:", round(sil_results, 3), "\n")
cat("Optimal k:", optimal_k, "\n")
```

```{r clustering-fit, fig.height=5}
# ── Fit the chosen k-means model ──
km_fit <- kmeans(cluster_vars, centers = optimal_k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
participant_profiles$cluster <- factor(km_fit$cluster)

# ── Cluster summary ──
cluster_summary <- participant_profiles %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_B = mean(pct_B), mean_N = mean(pct_N),
    mean_R = mean(pct_R), mean_K = mean(pct_K),
    mean_risk = mean(mean_risk),
    mean_rho  = mean(rho_risk_culp),
    mean_tau  = mean(tau, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_rpm  = mean(rpm_prop, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cluster_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = paste("K-means cluster profiles (k =", optimal_k, ")")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r cluster-viz, fig.height=5}
# ── PCA-based visualization of clusters ──
fviz_cluster(km_fit, data = cluster_vars, 
             geom = "point", ellipse = TRUE, 
             ellipse.type = "convex",
             palette = "grey",
             ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
```


## Risk Magnitude Mediation (Exploratory)

Does risk magnitude mediate the effect of vignette features on culpability?
That is, do features influence judgments by changing perceived risk, or do
they have direct effects beyond what risk explains?

The simplest test: compare feature coefficients in a model without risk
(direct + indirect effects combined) versus a model with risk (direct
effects only). A substantial reduction in feature coefficients when risk
is added suggests mediation.

```{r mediation}
# ── Model without risk: features only ──
m_features_only <- clmm(
  culpability_f ~ source_bin + package_bin + inquiry_bin +
                  payment_bin + location_bin + contents_bin + (1 | pid),
  data = d
)

# ── Compare feature coefficients: with vs. without risk ──
coef_no_risk <- summary(m_features_only)$coefficients
coef_w_risk  <- summary(m_full)$coefficients

feature_names <- c("source_bin", "package_bin", "inquiry_bin",
                   "payment_bin", "location_bin", "contents_bin")
feature_labels <- c("Source", "Package", "Inquiry", 
                    "Payment", "Location", "Contents")

mediation_table <- tibble(
  Feature = feature_labels,
  b_total  = coef_no_risk[feature_names, "Estimate"],
  b_direct = coef_w_risk[feature_names, "Estimate"],
  reduction_pct = (1 - b_direct / b_total) * 100
)

mediation_table %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 3, 3, 1),
        col.names = c("Feature", "b (no risk)", "b (with risk)", "% reduction"),
        caption = "Mediation check: coefficient reduction when risk is added") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

**Mediation interpretation.** A positive reduction means the feature effect
shrinks when risk is added, suggesting risk partially mediates that feature's
influence on culpability. Source and Package show the largest reductions (over
50% and 80% respectively), indicating that much of their effect operates
through perceived risk: participants who see a biker or duffel bag rate the
situation as riskier, and that elevated risk drives the culpability increase.

Location and Contents show *negative* reductions, meaning their coefficients
get *larger* (more negative) when risk is added. This is a suppression effect:
the feature and risk are correlated in one direction, but the feature pushes
culpability in the opposite direction once risk is controlled for. One
possibility is that participants who see "fentanyl" rate the scenario as
riskier (higher slider) but simultaneously infer that the defendant is less
culpable — a kind of "it was so obviously dangerous they must not have known"
reasoning. This suppression pattern, combined with the overall mediation
results, suggests that vignette features influence judgments through at least
two pathways: an indirect route through perceived risk (dominant for Source
and Package) and a direct route reflecting qualitative inferences about
intent (dominant for Payment).

```{r low-slider-exploration}
# ── Exploratory: do very low slider values function as "no awareness"? ──
# The MPC distinguishes negligence (failure to perceive risk) from
# recklessness (conscious disregard of perceived risk). If participants
# use the low end of the slider to indicate non-awareness, we should see
# an elevated proportion of Blamelessness and Negligence judgments at
# very low slider values.

d <- d %>%
  mutate(low_risk = slider_value <= 10)

low_risk_table <- d %>%
  group_by(low_risk) %>%
  count(judgment) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  dplyr::select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = judgment, values_from = pct, values_fill = 0)

cat("── Judgment distribution by slider range ──\n")
low_risk_table %>%
  mutate(low_risk = ifelse(low_risk, "Slider ≤ 10", "Slider > 10")) %>%
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Judgment proportions for low vs. higher risk ratings") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```


## Order and Learning Effects

Do judgments shift across the five vignettes within a session? If
participants are learning from the task or developing a response strategy,
we might see systematic position effects.

```{r order-effects}
# ── Mean culpability by presentation position ──
position_summary <- d %>%
  group_by(position) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_culp = mean(culpability),
    se_culp   = sd(culpability) / sqrt(n()),
    mean_risk = mean(slider_value),
    se_risk   = sd(slider_value) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

position_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean culpability and risk by presentation position") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

# ── Test position as a predictor in the CLMM ──
m_position <- clmm(
  culpability_f ~ slider_value + position + (1 | pid),
  data = d
)

pos_coef <- summary(m_position)$coefficients["position", ]
cat("Position effect in CLMM: b =", fmt_num(pos_coef["Estimate"], 3),
    ", z =", fmt_num(pos_coef["z value"], 2),
    ", p", fmt_p(pos_coef["Pr(>|z|)"]), "\n")
```


# Model Diagnostics

## Proportional Odds Assumption

The CLMM assumes proportional odds: the effect of each predictor on the
log-odds is the same across all three threshold transitions. A violation
would mean, for example, that risk matters more for the transition from
Negligence to Recklessness than for Blamelessness to Negligence.

We test this by fitting separate binary logistic models at each threshold
and comparing the risk coefficients. If they are roughly similar, the
assumption holds.

```{r proportional-odds}
# ── Threshold-specific models ──
# Create binary outcomes at each threshold:
#   Y1: culpability >= 2 (Negligence or higher vs. Blamelessness)
#   Y2: culpability >= 3 (Recklessness or higher vs. Negligence or lower)
#   Y3: culpability >= 4 (Knowledge vs. everything else)

d <- d %>%
  mutate(
    y_ge2 = as.integer(culpability >= 2),
    y_ge3 = as.integer(culpability >= 3),
    y_ge4 = as.integer(culpability >= 4)
  )

# Fit a logistic mixed model at each threshold.
m_t1 <- glmer(y_ge2 ~ slider_value + (1 | pid), data = d, family = binomial,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
m_t2 <- glmer(y_ge3 ~ slider_value + (1 | pid), data = d, family = binomial,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
m_t3 <- glmer(y_ge4 ~ slider_value + (1 | pid), data = d, family = binomial,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# Compare the risk coefficients.
threshold_coefs <- tibble(
  Threshold = c("≥ Negligence (1→2+)", "≥ Recklessness (2→3+)", "≥ Knowledge (3→4)"),
  b_risk = c(fixef(m_t1)["slider_value"], 
             fixef(m_t2)["slider_value"],
             fixef(m_t3)["slider_value"]),
  SE = c(sqrt(vcov(m_t1)["slider_value","slider_value"]),
         sqrt(vcov(m_t2)["slider_value","slider_value"]),
         sqrt(vcov(m_t3)["slider_value","slider_value"]))
) %>%
  mutate(
    ci_lo = b_risk - 1.96 * SE,
    ci_hi = b_risk + 1.96 * SE
  )

threshold_coefs %>%
  kable(digits = 4,
        col.names = c("Threshold", "b (risk)", "SE", "95% CI lo", "95% CI hi"),
        caption = "Risk coefficient at each threshold (proportional odds check)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r proportional-odds-diagnostic}
# ── Formal assessment ──
# The proportional odds assumption requires these three coefficients to be
# approximately equal. We check whether their 95% CIs overlap.

cat("── Proportional odds diagnostic ──\n")
cat("Risk coefficient at Threshold 1 (≥ Negligence):   ", 
    fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Risk coefficient at Threshold 2 (≥ Recklessness): ", 
    fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk[2], 4), "\n")
cat("Risk coefficient at Threshold 3 (≥ Knowledge):    ", 
    fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk[3], 4), "\n\n")

# Ratio of smallest to largest coefficient
ratio_3_1 <- threshold_coefs$b_risk[3] / threshold_coefs$b_risk[1]
cat("Ratio (Threshold 3 / Threshold 1):", fmt_num(ratio_3_1, 3), "\n\n")

# Do CIs of Threshold 1 and Threshold 3 overlap?
ci_overlap <- threshold_coefs$ci_lo[1] < threshold_coefs$ci_hi[3] &
              threshold_coefs$ci_lo[3] < threshold_coefs$ci_hi[1]

if (!ci_overlap & ratio_3_1 < 0.5) {
  cat("CONCLUSION: The proportional odds assumption is VIOLATED.\n")
  cat("The risk coefficient drops monotonically across thresholds, from\n")
  cat(fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk[1], 3), "at the lowest transition to",
      fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk[3], 3), "at the highest.\n")
  cat("The coefficient at the Knowledge threshold is roughly",
      round(1/ratio_3_1, 1), "times smaller\n")
  cat("than at the Negligence threshold (95% CIs do NOT overlap).\n\n")
  cat("This means risk perception is a strong discriminator between\n")
  cat("Blamelessness, Negligence, and Recklessness, but a much weaker\n")
  cat("discriminator at the top of the culpability scale. This is\n")
  cat("consistent with the H4 reversal (Knowledge trials having LOWER\n")
  cat("risk ratings than Recklessness trials) and suggests that the\n")
  cat("Knowledge category is driven by qualitative cues (e.g., payment)\n")
  cat("rather than quantitative risk perception.\n")
} else {
  cat("CONCLUSION: The proportional odds assumption is approximately satisfied.\n")
  cat("Risk coefficients across thresholds:", 
      paste(fmt_num(threshold_coefs$b_risk, 3), collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("95% CIs", ifelse(ci_overlap, "overlap", "do NOT overlap"), 
      "; ratio =", fmt_num(ratio_3_1, 3), "\n")
}
```

```{r proportional-odds-plot, fig.height=4}
# ── Visualize the proportional odds check ──
threshold_coefs %>%
  mutate(Threshold = factor(Threshold, levels = Threshold)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Threshold, y = b_risk)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = coef(m_risk)["slider_value"], 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi), width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = coef(m_risk)["slider_value"], 
           label = "CLMM pooled estimate", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.8, 
           size = 3, color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Risk Coefficient (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))
```


## ROC Analysis for Threshold Models

As suggested during review, we compute ROC curves and AUC values for each
threshold-specific logistic model. This provides a complementary measure
of how well the risk slider discriminates at each transition point.

```{r roc-analysis, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
# ── ROC curves for each threshold model ──
# Extract predicted probabilities from each threshold-specific GLMM.
d$pred_t1 <- predict(m_t1, type = "response")
d$pred_t2 <- predict(m_t2, type = "response")
d$pred_t3 <- predict(m_t3, type = "response")

roc_t1 <- roc(d$y_ge2, d$pred_t1, quiet = TRUE)
roc_t2 <- roc(d$y_ge3, d$pred_t2, quiet = TRUE)
roc_t3 <- roc(d$y_ge4, d$pred_t3, quiet = TRUE)

cat("── AUC by threshold ──\n")
cat("≥ Negligence (B vs. N+):    AUC =", fmt_num(auc(roc_t1), 3), "\n")
cat("≥ Recklessness (N- vs. R+): AUC =", fmt_num(auc(roc_t2), 3), "\n")
cat("≥ Knowledge (R- vs. K):     AUC =", fmt_num(auc(roc_t3), 3), "\n")
cat("\nAUC declines at the Knowledge threshold, consistent with the\n")
cat("proportional odds violation and the H4 risk reversal.\n")
```


## Vignette Feature Balance

The minimization algorithm should produce roughly balanced factor levels.
We verify this here.

```{r feature-balance}
# ── Check that each binary feature is approximately 50/50 ──
balance_table <- d %>%
  summarise(across(c(source_bin, package_bin, inquiry_bin, 
                     payment_bin, location_bin, contents_bin),
                   ~ mean(.x) * 100)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Feature", values_to = "Pct_Level_1") %>%
  mutate(
    Feature = recode(Feature,
      "source_bin"   = "Source (biker)",
      "package_bin"  = "Package (duffel bag)",
      "inquiry_bin"  = "Inquiry (source tells)",
      "payment_bin"  = "Payment ($1000)",
      "location_bin" = "Location (Mexico)",
      "contents_bin" = "Contents (fentanyl)"
    ),
    Pct_Level_0 = 100 - Pct_Level_1
  )

balance_table %>%
  kable(digits = 1, col.names = c("Feature", "% Level 1", "% Level 0"),
        caption = "Feature balance (ideal: 50/50)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r fig-predicted-probs, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# ── Figure 3: Predicted probability curves from CLMM with 95% CIs ──
# Uses color + linetype for online/print compatibility, plus geom_textpath
# labels directly on curves per Jaime's suggestion.
# Each label is placed at a different hjust to avoid the crossing zone.

# Label placement: position each label where its curve has breathing room.
#   Blamelessness peaks left  → label early (hjust 0.12)
#   Negligence peaks ~30      → label at 0.28
#   Recklessness peaks ~75    → label at 0.72
#   Knowledge rises right     → label late (0.88)
label_hjust <- c(
  "Blamelessness" = 0.12,
  "Negligence"    = 0.28,
  "Recklessness"  = 0.80,
  "Knowledge"     = 0.60
)

# Helper to build the plot with a given color palette
build_fig3 <- function(color_pal) {
  p <- ggplot(pred_with_ci, aes(x = slider, y = probability,
                                 color = judgment, linetype = judgment)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi, fill = judgment, group = judgment),
                alpha = 0.15, color = NA)
  
  # Add each curve's label at its own position
  for (j in names(label_hjust)) {
    p <- p + geom_textpath(
      data = pred_with_ci %>% filter(judgment == j),
      aes(label = judgment), linewidth = 0.9,
      size = 3, hjust = label_hjust[j], text_smoothing = 50
    )
  }
  
  p + scale_color_manual(values = color_pal) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = color_pal) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = judgment_linetypes) +
    labs(x = "Risk Slider (0–100)", y = "Predicted Probability") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
    guides(color = "none", fill = "none", linetype = "none") +
    theme_pub
}

fig3_color <- build_fig3(judgment_colors)
fig3_bw    <- build_fig3(judgment_grays)

fig3_color
save_dual(fig3_color, fig3_bw, "fig3_predicted_probabilities", 7, 5)
```

# Summary

```{r summary-table}
# ── Bring all hypothesis results into one table ──

# For H2, report both CLMM z and ρ for completeness.
h2_test_str <- paste0("CLMM z = ", fmt_num(risk_z, 2),
                       "; ρ = ", fmt_num(rho_test$estimate, 3))
h2_es_str   <- paste0("OR/10pt = ", fmt_num(exp(risk_b * 10), 3),
                       "; β_std = ", fmt_num(risk_b_std, 3))

# For H3, report the CLMM z for payment.
h3_z   <- summary(m_full)$coefficients["payment_bin", "z value"]
h3_p   <- summary(m_full)$coefficients["payment_bin", "Pr(>|z|)"]
h3_d   <- summary(m_full)$coefficients["payment_bin", "Estimate"] * sqrt(3) / pi
h3_or  <- exp(summary(m_full)$coefficients["payment_bin", "Estimate"])

# For H4, report two-tailed p since the effect is reversed.
h4_test_str <- paste0("t = ", fmt_num(t_val, 2), 
                       "; d = ", fmt_num(cohens_d_rk, 3))

summary_results <- tribble(
  ~Hypothesis, ~Test, ~`Effect Size`, ~p, ~Decision,
  
  "H1: Non-uniform",
  paste0("χ²(3) = ", round(chi_adj, 1), " (DEFF-adj)"),
  paste0("w = ", fmt_num(as.numeric(cohens_w), 3)),
  fmt_p(p_adj),
  "Supported",
  
  "H2: Risk–culpability",
  h2_test_str,
  h2_es_str,
  fmt_p(risk_p),
  "Supported",
  
  "H3: Payment bias",
  paste0("z = ", fmt_num(h3_z, 2)),
  paste0("d ≈ ", fmt_num(h3_d, 3), "; OR = ", fmt_num(h3_or, 3)),
  fmt_p(h3_p),
  "Supported",
  
  "H4: R vs. K (exploratory)",
  h4_test_str,
  paste0("b = ", fmt_num(rk_coef["Estimate"], 2)),
  fmt_p(p_two_tailed),
  "Reversed (K < R)"
)

summary_results %>%
  kable(caption = "Summary of hypothesis tests") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```
